The most prominent example of explicit national origin-based immigration quotas in U.S. history was the Immigration Act of 1924, also known as the Johnson-Reed Act, which built on the earlier Emergency Quota Act of 1921. The law assigned each country an annual immigration quota calculated as a percentage of the number of foreign-born residents from that country recorded in the 1890 U.S. census. Because the 1890 population was overwhelmingly composed of immigrants from Northern and Western Europe, the formula effectively allocated the largest visa allotments to countries such as Britain, Ireland, Germany, and Scandinavia. Immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe (Italy, Poland, Greece, the Balkans) was sharply restricted, and immigration from Asia was already largely barred by earlier laws such as the Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) and the Asiatic Barred Zone (1917).   1. Preserving the "racial composition" of the population. Many supporters openly stated that they wished to maintain the United States as a country of predominantly Northern European stock, drawing on popular pseudo-scientific theories of the era.
